card.law_is_about: Adding wolves to federal hunting law and regulating regular hunting and targeted removals.
card.they_want: Broader regular wolf hunting, with fewer conservation-status obstacles.
card.they_claim: An absence of favourable conservation status among German wolves cannot justify opposition to regular hunting, because the whole European population is decisive.
card.the_problem: The cited judgment expressly requires local and national assessment. Cross-border exchange can support favourable status; a favourable European population does not replace the national assessment.

claim_quote.translation_en: Translation: An alleged absence of favourable conservation status among German wolves can therefore in no way serve as a reason against regular wolf hunting.

counter_quote.translation_en: Translation of fragment: exist and be assessed at local and national level

correction: C-629/23 requires favourable conservation status to exist and be assessed primarily and necessarily at local and national level. Paragraph48 expressly applies that principle to Article14 management of AnnexV species. Paragraphs52–64 allow relevant cross-border demographic and genetic exchange to inform that assessment, including where an isolated national population would not be viable. They do not make an unfavourable national status irrelevant merely because the wider European population is favourable.
effect: Removes the stated legal basis for dismissing the German conservation-status condition in the argument for regular hunting. It does not establish the outcome of any particular hunting application.
limits: The judgment does not require each country’s wolves to be biologically self-sufficient: paragraph55 expressly allows continuous exchange to support favourable national status. The author’s earlier phrase about local wolves not being favourable entirely on their own is compatible with that point. The finding concerns the later categorical dismissal of German status, not the legitimacy of considering European connections. It does not determine Germany’s actual conservation status, ecological population boundaries, hunting effectiveness, the legality of every targeted removal, or the desirability of the bill. No intent is inferred.
context_and_alternatives: Read all3physical submission pages, including the author’s separate ecological reasons for hunting, preference for juvenile removal, and desire to place operational guidelines in ordinances.

The strongest benign reading is that the author objects to treating Germany as an isolated biological population. The cited judgment supports considering cross-border exchange, but expressly preserves the local and national legal assessment; the later categorical conclusion goes beyond that reading.

The case concerns Estonia, where wolves already fell under AnnexV. Its Article14 reasoning is relevant to the proposed post-reclassification German framework; no claim is made that all factual circumstances are identical.
The population-size assertions and the claim that all European populations exchange genes were not independently determined here. They are not separate findings.
